title: Rusty Budgets: core concepts
description: A tour of the domain model and architecture: the Budget aggregate, CQRS events, tags/items/transactions, and the tagging + transfer-resolution UI that drives day-to-day use.

steps.title: Workspace layout
steps.explanation:
## Start here

Rusty Budgets is a full-stack Rust app built with **Dioxus** (web/desktop/mobile from one codebase), a custom JSON file database called **JoyDB**, and a hand-rolled **CQRS + event sourcing** layer.

The workspace splits into:
- `api/` — domain model, events, server functions
- `ui/` — shared Dioxus components
- `web/`, `desktop/`, `mobile/` — platform entry points
- `cqrs_macros/` — proc macros for event handling

The intended user workflow is: **Setup → Import → Tag & Create Rules → Create Budget Items → Day-to-day budget work**. This tour follows that same order.

steps.title: Budget: the aggregate root
steps.explanation:
## Everything hangs off `Budget`

`Budget` is the single **aggregate root** (event-sourcing terminology: the consistency boundary that all events target). It owns:

- `items` — budget categories (`BudgetItem`)
- `periods` — one `BudgetPeriod` per calendar month
- `accounts` — bank accounts
- `match_rules` — auto-categorisation rules
- `currency`, `month_begins_on` — budget-wide settings

Above it, `pub_events_enum!` generates `BudgetEvent`, an enum wrapping every event type that can happen to a budget — `TransactionTagged`, `ItemAdded`, `TagClassified`, and so on. **State is never mutated directly; it's always the result of applying one of these events.**

steps.title: The event-sourcing framework
steps.explanation:
## Aggregate + DomainEvent

Two traits define the whole framework:

- **`Aggregate`** — anything with an id and a version that evolves over time (`Budget` implements this).
- **`DomainEvent<A>`** — anything that can `apply()` itself to an aggregate and return the id of whatever it affected.

Every mutation in the app is: validate → construct an event → `apply()` it → persist it. There's no direct field mutation from command handlers — replaying the event log is how state gets rebuilt.

steps.title: A concrete event: TransactionTagged
steps.explanation:
## One event, start to finish

This is the smallest complete example of the pattern:

- `TransactionTagged { budget_id, tx_id, tag_id }` — the event's data (just enough to replay it)
- `#[domain_event(aggregate = "Budget")]` — the `cqrs_macros::DomainEvent` derive generates the boilerplate `Handler` trait and wiring
- `do_transaction_tagged_impl` — the **command**: validates the transaction and tag exist, then builds the event (fails closed, never mutates)
- `apply_do_transaction_tagged` — the **event application**: the only place that actually sets `tx.tag_id`

Every other event file in `api/src/events/` (26 of them, listed in the `BudgetEvent` enum) follows this exact shape.

steps.title: Tag: periodicity lives here, not on the item
steps.explanation:
## Cost behavior is a property of the tag

`CostKind` decides how a tag's spending is budgeted:

- **`Recurring(Periodicity)`** — a billed commitment (rent, annual insurance). It periodises: a 12,000 kr/year bill contributes 1,000 kr/month and builds a **buffer** between bills.
- **`Variable`** — everyday spending (groceries) with no cadence, budgeted per month as it happens.

The key design decision: "Electricity" is *inherently* monthly, "Dog Insurance" is *inherently* annual — that's a fact about the category, not about any one transaction or budget item, so it's attached to the `Tag`.

steps.title: Tag struct + backward-compatible loading
steps.explanation:
## Tags are never hard-deleted

`deleted: bool` is a soft-delete flag — tags must stay historically intact so old transactions and reports still resolve correctly. `needs_review` and `explicitly_classified` track whether a tag's `CostKind` was chosen by the user or just inferred from a legacy field, which matters because of how old snapshots load (next step).

steps.title: Migrating old data without a migration
steps.explanation:
## No SQL means no ALTER TABLE

Because aggregates are persisted as JSON snapshots plus a tail of replayed events, adding a required field would break every existing budget on load. `TagRepr` is a permissive deserialization shim: new fields (`cost_kind`, `matching`) win when present, otherwise they're derived from the legacy `periodicity` field. This pattern — an intermediate `*Repr` struct — is how the domain model evolves without a schema migration step.

steps.title: BudgetItem: grouping tags into a budget line
steps.explanation:
## One item, many tags

A `BudgetItem` is a named budget line (e.g. "Transport") that references one or more tags by `tag_ids: Vec<Uuid>` — so "Transport" can bundle the "Car", "Bus Pass", and "Train" tags into a single budgeted amount. `budgeting_type` (Income/Expense/Savings/InternalTransfer) and `buffer_target` (the rolling-buffer amount for recurring costs) live here too.

steps.title: MatchRule: auto-categorisation
steps.explanation:
## How tagging one transaction tags many

When a user tags a transaction, the app auto-creates a `MatchRule` from tokenised fragments of its description (`transaction_key`). Every future untagged transaction is checked against the set of `match_rules` on `Budget` — a match applies `tag_id` automatically. Tokenisation is Swedish-localised (filters Swedish stopwords and dates), since transaction descriptions come from Swedish bank exports.

steps.title: Money: never mix currencies
steps.explanation:
## Cents, not floats

`Money` stores an `i64` in minor units (cents/öre) plus a `Currency`. This avoids float rounding errors entirely. Arithmetic between two `Money` values of different currencies panics rather than silently producing a wrong number — correctness over convenience, since this is a budgeting app.

steps.title: Server functions: the API surface
steps.explanation:
## #[server] functions are the whole backend

Dioxus's `#[server]` macro turns each function into a client-callable RPC endpoint, backed by real server code. `get_untagged_transactions` fetches a batch for the tagging workflow; `tag_transaction` applies a tag and fires rule evaluation; `resolve_transfer_pair` is the internal-transfer resolution endpoint we'll see wired to the UI next. All of them return a `BudgetViewModel` — a read-optimized projection, never the raw aggregate.

steps.title: The tagging workflow UI
steps.explanation:
## Where the domain model meets the screen

`TagTransactionsView` is the core day-one UX loop: untagged transactions are shown in batches of `BATCH_SIZE` (10), the user picks or creates a tag, and behind the scenes `create_tag` → `tag_transaction` → `apply_all_rules` chains through the server functions and events we've just walked through. It's mounted in the budget overview whenever there are untagged transactions.

steps.title: Detecting potential internal transfers
steps.explanation:
## Same amount, different account, few days apart

`potential_internal_transfers()` finds pairs of unallocated, untagged transactions with matching absolute amounts across different accounts within a short window — likely one "move money" action seen as two bank-side transactions (e.g. moving money to a savings account). These are excluded from the regular tagging flow and resolved separately.

steps.title: Resolving a transfer pair
steps.explanation:
## Savings deposits aren't a second expense

`TransferPairCard` offers two resolutions: mark the pair as a neutral internal float (ignore both sides), or — when the incoming leg lands in a `Savings`-type account — tag the *outgoing* leg as a savings contribution and ignore the incoming receipt. This correctly models savings: the deduction from checking is the budget event; the deposit is just where it landed, not a second thing to budget for.
